title: Grade 4 HINDU RELIGIOUS EDUCATION — 2.1 Enlightened Beings

pages.lesson:
PAGE 1: Overview

OVERVIEW
========

Enlightened Beings are holy teachers and divine forms whose lives guide people towards truth and goodness. In this sub-strand you will meet Narsimha Avtar, Parshavnath, the childhood of Lord Buddha, and Sri Guru Ram Das Ji. You will name what each one gave the world and practise those teachings in ordinary school life.

## Strand 2.0: Manifestations of Paramatma
Sub-strand 2.1: Enlightened Beings
Suggested lessons: 10

## Learning outcomes
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) identify the contributions of Enlightened Beings for inspiration
b) implement teachings of Enlightened Beings for righteous living
c) appreciate the teachings of Enlightened Beings for spiritual and moral growth

## What this sub-strand covers
• Narsimha Avtar
• Parshavnath
• Lord Buddha- His childhood
• Sri Guru Ram Das ji

## Key inquiry questions
1. Why are Enlightened Beings considered Divine?
2. What do we learn from the life of Prince Siddhartha?
3. How are the teachings of Sri Guru Ram Das Ji applicable in modern society?

## Core competencies
• Digital Literacy: Learner interacts with digital literacy when matching the Enlightened Beings with the reforms done by each (through dragging and dropping on digital device).
• Learning to learn: Learner learns independently when participating in short essay writing competition on Enlightened Beings.

## Values
• Respect: Learner enhances open-mindedness when performing skits based on the reforms done by Enlightened Beings.

## Pertinent and contemporary issues
• Citizenship: Learner is sensitised on human rights and responsibilities while matching the Enlightened Beings with the reforms done by each.

## Links to other learning areas
• Learner is able to link the skills of performing skits based on the reforms done by Enlightened Beings to the creative skills learnt in Creative Arts.

## Source
• KICD Grade 4 Hindu Religious Education Curriculum Design (Revised 2024) — Strand 2.0 Manifestations of Paramatma, Sub-strand 2.1 Enlightened Beings

PAGE 2: Lesson 1: Who Enlightened Beings are

LESSON 1: WHO ENLIGHTENED BEINGS ARE
====================================

## What you will learn
• Explain what is meant by an Enlightened Being in this sub-strand.
• Name the four Enlightened Beings to be studied.

Curriculum outcomes: a) identify the contributions of Enlightened Beings for inspiration; c) appreciate the teachings of Enlightened Beings for spiritual and moral growth

## Introduction
Stories of brave and holy lives are told at home, in the mandir, in the gurdwara and in the derasar. Hindu Religious Education calls some of these figures Enlightened Beings because their lives shine with truth and help other people live better.

## Notes
### A light for other people
To be enlightened means to see clearly what is true and what is right. An Enlightened Being may be a divine form of Paramatma, such as an avtar, or a human teacher who woke up to truth and then taught others. In both cases, people of faith look to that being for inspiration. Inspiration means a good example that makes you want to live bravely and kindly.

These beings are called divine by their communities because their lives are not ordinary stories of fame. They protect the weak, tell the truth, give up comfort for the sake of others, or build places where all people can worship together. Remembering them is a way of remembering God and goodness.

### The four you will study
This sub-strand names four:
- **Narsimha Avtar** — the man-lion form of Lord Vishnu in Sanatan tradition, remembered for protecting the child devotee Prahlad
- **Parshavnath** — the twenty-third Tirthankara of the Jains, a teacher of non-violence
- **Lord Buddha in his childhood** — Prince Siddhartha, before he became the Buddha
- **Sri Guru Ram Das Ji** — the fourth Guru of the Sikhs, remembered for humility and service

Each belongs to one of the four faiths you study. Learning one does not cancel the others. A respectful learner can admire Prahlad's courage and also admire Guru Ram Das Ji's service.

### How we will learn
You will hear short stories, match each being with a reform or a teaching, and try one teaching in class. A reform here means a change towards a fairer or holier way of living. Do not mix up their names. Narsimha is not a Sikh Guru, and Guru Ram Das Ji is not a Tirthankara.

## Key words
• enlightened — awake to truth; a guide whose life shows what is right
• avtar — a divine descent; a form in which God appears, in Sanatan teaching
• inspiration — a good example that encourages you to live better

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A learner says all four Enlightened Beings were Sikh Gurus. How should the list be corrected?

Working:
1. Only Sri Guru Ram Das Ji is a Sikh Guru, the fourth.
2. Narsimha Avtar belongs to Sanatan tradition.
3. Parshavnath is a Jain Tirthankara, and Prince Siddhartha is the future Buddha.

Answer: They come from four faiths: Sanatan, Jain, Buddhist and Sikh, one figure each.

## Activity: Match the Enlightened Being to the faith
You will need: Four name cards, Four faith cards
1. Spread out cards for Narsimha Avtar, Parshavnath, Prince Siddhartha and Sri Guru Ram Das Ji.
2. Match each name to Sanatan, Jain, Buddhist or Sikh.
3. With a partner, say one reason people of that faith honour the figure. If you are unsure, leave a question mark and listen to the coming lessons.
4. Help a classmate who needs the cards read aloud so that everyone can join the match.

## Practice
1. What does it mean to call someone an inspiration?
2. Name the four Enlightened Beings in this sub-strand.
3. Which of the four is a Jain Tirthankara?

## Summary
• Enlightened Beings guide people by their truth and goodness.
• This sub-strand studies Narsimha Avtar, Parshavnath, the childhood of the Buddha and Sri Guru Ram Das Ji.
• Each figure is kept with the correct faith.

### Answers to practice
1. Their example encourages other people to live in a better way.
2. Narsimha Avtar, Parshavnath, Lord Buddha as a child (Prince Siddhartha), and Sri Guru Ram Das Ji.
3. Parshavnath.

PAGE 3: Lesson 2: Narsimha Avtar and Prahlad

LESSON 2: NARSIMHA AVTAR AND PRAHLAD
====================================

## What you will learn
• Retell the story of Prahlad and Narsimha Avtar in the correct order.
• State what this avtar contributed for people of faith.

Curriculum outcomes: a) identify the contributions of Enlightened Beings for inspiration; c) appreciate the teachings of Enlightened Beings for spiritual and moral growth

## Introduction
Some children are pressed to do what they know is wrong. The Sanatan story of Prahlad tells of a boy who kept loving Lord Vishnu even when a powerful king tried to stop him. Vishnu came as Narsimha Avtar to protect him.

## Notes
### The king and the boy
Hiranyakashipu was a powerful king who wanted everyone to worship him. He had received a boon that made him feel safe from death: he was not to be killed by man or beast, not by day or by night, not indoors or outdoors, not on the earth or in the sky, and not by any weapon. His pride grew until he hated Lord Vishnu.

His own son, Prahlad, loved Vishnu. The boy chanted Vishnu's name at school and refused to say that the king was God. Hiranyakashipu tried again and again to turn him or to harm him. Prahlad stayed calm and faithful.

### The appearance of Narsimha
At last the king pointed to a pillar and mocked the idea that Vishnu could be in it. The pillar broke open. Narsimha appeared: a form that was neither a man nor a beast alone, but a man-lion. It was twilight, neither day nor night. Narsimha met the king on the threshold, which is neither fully inside nor fully outside, placed him on his lap, which is neither earth nor sky, and used claws rather than a weapon. The cruel king was destroyed. Prahlad was safe, and he asked mercy even for his father.

### The contribution
Narsimha Avtar is remembered as God's protection of a faithful child and as the defeat of pride and cruelty. The contribution is not a licence to be violent. It is a promise, in Sanatan teaching, that Paramatma stands with those who hold to truth, and that no boon can protect a person who harms the innocent.

Tell the story with respect. Do not act the killing in a frightening way in class. The part to copy is Prahlad's faith and his refusal to call a bully a god.

## Key words
• Narsimha — the man-lion avtar of Lord Vishnu
• Prahlad — the young devotee who stayed faithful to Vishnu
• boon — a special gift or promise, often from a deity after penance

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Why did Narsimha appear as a man-lion at twilight, on the threshold, using claws?

Working:
1. The king's boon blocked death by man or beast, by day or night, indoors or outdoors, on earth or in the sky, and by a weapon.
2. Each detail of the avtar meets the boon without breaking it.
3. The story teaches that pride cannot fence God out.

Answer: So that the proud king's boon could not stop the protection of Prahlad.

## Activity: Listen and retell the story of Narsimha
You will need: The story as told by a teacher, parent or audio recording
1. Listen to the story of Prahlad and Narsimha from your teacher, a parent or an audio device.
2. In groups, retell it in order: the proud king, the faithful boy, the pillar, the avtar, the safety of Prahlad.
3. Write one sentence on what this Enlightened Being contributes: protection of faith and the fall of cruelty.
4. Do not act violent blows. If you perform a sketch, end with Prahlad's prayer.

## Practice
1. Who was Prahlad, and whom did he worship?
2. What form did Lord Vishnu take to protect Prahlad?
3. What is the main contribution of this story for believers?

## Summary
• Prahlad stayed devoted to Vishnu when the king demanded worship for himself.
• Narsimha Avtar, the man-lion, protected Prahlad and ended the king's cruelty.
• The teaching is faith, courage and the defeat of pride.

### Answers to practice
1. He was the son of King Hiranyakashipu, and he worshipped Lord Vishnu.
2. Narsimha, the man-lion avtar.
3. It teaches that God protects a person who stays faithful, and that pride and cruelty do not last.

PAGE 4: Lesson 3: Living Prahlad's courage

LESSON 3: LIVING PRAHLAD'S COURAGE
==================================

## What you will learn
• Apply the teaching of Prahlad to situations at school.
• Choose truth and respect without insulting people who are powerful.

Curriculum outcomes: b) implement teachings of Enlightened Beings for righteous living; c) appreciate the teachings of Enlightened Beings for spiritual and moral growth

## Introduction
You may never face a king, but you may face a friend who says, 'Cheat with us, or we will leave you out.' Prahlad's story is told so that learners can answer that kind of pressure with a steady mind.

## Notes
### What to copy, and what not to copy
Prahlad did not gather a gang to fight his father. He told the truth, kept his prayer, and trusted Vishnu. Narsimha's appearance was God's act, not a plan for children to scratch or hit people. When we implement this teaching we practise faith, honesty and courage of speech. We do not practise cruelty.

### School situations
- Someone tells you to laugh at a classmate's faith or at the way they pray. You can refuse and change the subject.
- A group wants you to lie to the teacher about a broken window. You can tell the truth calmly.
- An older learner says you must give them your food. You can say no and walk to a teacher. Prahlad also spoke up; he did not pretend the king was right.
- You yourself have been proud and unkind. The story warns Hiranyakashipu's pride as much as it praises Prahlad. Apologise and start again.

### A calm voice
Courage can be quiet. A firm sentence is enough: 'I will not lie,' or 'I will not insult his prayer.' Shouting insults back is not devotion. Prahlad kept honouring Vishnu. He did not become a second bully.

### Appreciation
To appreciate this teaching is to be glad that faith can live inside a child, not only inside adults. Say thank you when you hear the story at home. If your family is not Sanatan, you can still respect the story and take the moral of honesty. Respect is part of spiritual growth.

## Key words
• implement — to put a teaching into practice
• devotion — steady love and loyalty towards God

## Worked examples

### Example 1
During group work, three learners copy answers and tell Asha to copy too, or they will say she is proud. What response fits Prahlad's example?

Working:
1. Copying and then lying is the wrong Prahlad refused, in a school form.
2. Asha can say no without insulting the group.
3. If they threaten her, she tells the teacher. She does not scratch or hit them.

Answer: She refuses to copy, speaks calmly, and reports the threat if it continues.

## Activity: A short skit on standing for the truth
You will need: Space to act, Three sentence cards
1. In small groups, choose one school pressure: cheating, mocking a faith, or taking someone's food.
2. Act a short skit in which one learner refuses calmly, as Prahlad refused the king's order.
3. End the skit with a helpful action, such as telling a teacher or apologising.
4. After each skit, the class names the teaching that was implemented.

## Practice
1. Name one way a learner can implement Prahlad's teaching at school.
2. Why should the class not copy the violent part of the Narsimha story?
3. What pride is warned against in the story of Hiranyakashipu?

## Summary
• Prahlad's example for school is truth, prayer and a calm refusal.
• Narsimha's act is God's, not a model for fighting.
• Appreciating the story means respecting devotion and rejecting pride.

### Answers to practice
1. Refuse to cheat or to mock someone's faith, and speak the truth calmly.
2. That moment belongs to the avtar's protection of Prahlad. Children are taught faith and courage, not cruelty.
3. The pride of demanding worship for yourself and harming a person who stays faithful to God.

PAGE 5: Lesson 4: Parshavnath, the twenty-third Tirthankara

LESSON 4: PARSHAVNATH, THE TWENTY-THIRD TIRTHANKARA
===================================================

## What you will learn
• Identify Parshavnath and his main teaching of non-violence.
• Give one way to practise that teaching.

Curriculum outcomes: a) identify the contributions of Enlightened Beings for inspiration; b) implement teachings of Enlightened Beings for righteous living

## Introduction
Long before modern wildlife clubs, Jain teachers were already saying that a small animal has a life you must not treat lightly. Parshavnath is honoured as the twenty-third Tirthankara, a guide who crossed beyond selfishness and showed others the way.

## Notes
### A Tirthankara
In Jain teaching, a Tirthankara is a person who has conquered anger, pride, greed and illusion and who builds a ford, a safe crossing, for others. Parshavnath is the twenty-third. Lord Mahavira, whom you meet when you study scriptures, is the twenty-fourth. Parshavnath is often shown with a canopy of snake hoods above him. The serpent is his emblem. It recalls a traditional account in which a serpent king sheltered him while he meditated, when he was attacked for his calm refusal to harm living beings.

### What he taught
Parshavnath taught householders and monks to restrain themselves. Four great restraints are remembered from his teaching:
- **Ahimsa** — do not injure living beings by thought, word or action
- **Satya** — speak the truth
- **Asteya** — do not steal or take what is not given
- **Aparigraha** — do not pile up more than you need

These are reforms of ordinary human habits. People often hurt others when they are angry, lie to escape trouble, take what they want, and cling to things. Parshavnath's contribution is a clear path of self-control.

### Implement ahimsa at Grade 4
You can practise without becoming a monk. Carry insects out of the classroom on a paper instead of crushing them when it is safe to do so. Do not throw stones at birds or dogs. Do not tear leaves off a living tree for fun. Speak in a way that does not wound a classmate. Ahimsa begins with the creatures and people you can reach today.

Appreciate this teaching by speaking of Parshavnath with his correct title, Tirthankara, and by not drawing his emblem as a joke.

## Key words
• Tirthankara — a Jain spiritual teacher who has crossed over and shows others the way
• Parshavnath — the twenty-third Jain Tirthankara, teacher of non-violence
• aparigraha — not holding on to more possessions than you need

## Worked examples

### Example 1
On the way home, learners hit a stray dog with sticks and laugh. Which restraint of Parshavnath does this break, and what should they do?

Working:
1. Harming an animal breaks ahimsa.
2. They should stop at once and leave the dog alone.
3. If the dog is hurt or dangerous, they tell an adult instead of attacking it.

Answer: It breaks ahimsa. They should stop, and tell an adult if the animal needs help.

## Activity: Match Parshavnath with his reforms
You will need: Cards for the four restraints, A picture of the snake emblem if one is available
1. Read a short account of Parshavnath told by your teacher or played on an audio device.
2. Match him with ahimsa, satya, asteya and aparigraha, and say each meaning in simple English.
3. Each learner chooses one restraint and writes one action they will do this week.
4. Assist a classmate who needs the words read aloud so they can make the same match.

## Practice
1. Who is Parshavnath?
2. What does ahimsa mean?
3. Name two restraints taught by Parshavnath besides ahimsa.

## Summary
• Parshavnath is the twenty-third Jain Tirthankara.
• He taught ahimsa, satya, asteya and aparigraha.
• Learners practise non-violence towards people, animals and plants.

### Answers to practice
1. The twenty-third Tirthankara in Jain tradition.
2. Non-violence: not harming living beings by thought, word or action.
3. Any two of satya (truth), asteya (not stealing) and aparigraha (not grabbing more than you need).

PAGE 6: Lesson 5: The childhood of Prince Siddhartha

LESSON 5: THE CHILDHOOD OF PRINCE SIDDHARTHA
============================================

## What you will learn
• Describe Prince Siddhartha's birth and sheltered childhood.
• Explain what his early life contributed to the story of the Buddha.

Curriculum outcomes: a) identify the contributions of Enlightened Beings for inspiration; c) appreciate the teachings of Enlightened Beings for spiritual and moral growth

## Introduction
Before he was called the Buddha, he was a prince in a palace. The key question of this sub-strand asks what we learn from the life of Prince Siddhartha. We begin with his childhood, not with later teachings he had not yet given.

## Notes
### Birth at Lumbini
Buddhist tradition says Prince Siddhartha Gautama was born at Lumbini. His father was King Suddhodana of the Shakya people, and his mother was Queen Maya. She died soon after his birth, and he was raised with love by Mahaprajapati Gautami, his mother's sister and the king's other queen. Wise visitors predicted that the child would become either a great ruler or a great sage.

### A palace without suffering in sight
The king wanted his son to choose the life of a ruler, so the boy was surrounded with comfort, beautiful gardens, fine clothes and pleasant company. He was trained in the skills of a prince. He was not cruel. Stories of his youth show a thoughtful boy who did not enjoy hurting living beings. He later married Yashodhara, and they had a son, Rahula. That family life still belongs to his early years, before he left the palace.

### What the comfort could not hide
As a young man he went out and saw four sights that his sheltered childhood had kept away: an old person, a sick person, a dead person, and a wandering holy man who looked peaceful. The first three showed him that comfort cannot cancel suffering. The fourth showed him a life given to seeking truth. He left the palace to understand suffering and the way beyond it. Years later, seated under the Boddhi tree, he awakened and was called the Buddha, the Awakened One.

### The contribution of the childhood story
The childhood itself is a gift to learners. It shows a child who had everything and still cared about pain that was not his own. People honour him as an Enlightened Being because that concern grew into a lifetime of teaching kindness, mindfulness and an end to cruelty. You do not need his palace in order to notice when someone in your class is left out or hurt.

## Key words
• Siddhartha — the prince who later became the Buddha
• Lumbini — the birthplace of Prince Siddhartha in Buddhist tradition
• Buddha — the Awakened One

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A learner says Prince Siddhartha was born poor and never lived in a palace. What does the childhood story actually say?

Working:
1. He was the son of King Suddhodana and Queen Maya.
2. He grew up with comfort in the palace and was protected from sights of suffering.
3. He left that comfort later, after seeing old age, sickness, death and a holy man.

Answer: He was a prince raised in comfort, and he left the palace when he saw suffering.

## Activity: Story of Prince Siddhartha's early life
You will need: A short reading or audio from the teacher
1. Listen to the childhood of Prince Siddhartha told by a resource person, a parent or an audio device.
2. Draw four small pictures: the birth and care by Mahaprajapati, life in the palace, the four sights, and a kind action of your own.
3. Under the drawing, write what we learn from his early life.
4. Watch only a film or video your teacher has chosen. Discuss one true fact from it, not a made-up scene.

## Practice
1. Where was Prince Siddhartha born, according to Buddhist tradition?
2. Who raised him after his mother, Queen Maya, died?
3. What four sights moved him to leave the palace?

## Summary
• Prince Siddhartha was born at Lumbini and raised in a palace after Queen Maya died.
• Comfort did not stop him from caring when he later saw suffering.
• His childhood leads towards his awakening as the Buddha.

### Answers to practice
1. At Lumbini.
2. Mahaprajapati Gautami.
3. An old person, a sick person, a dead person and a holy man.

PAGE 7: Lesson 6: What Prince Siddhartha teaches us now

LESSON 6: WHAT PRINCE SIDDHARTHA TEACHES US NOW
===============================================

## What you will learn
• List lessons from Prince Siddhartha's life for a Grade 4 learner.
• Show one of those lessons in a class activity.

Curriculum outcomes: b) implement teachings of Enlightened Beings for righteous living; c) appreciate the teachings of Enlightened Beings for spiritual and moral growth

## Introduction
A prince who notices suffering is a useful teacher for a school compound. Someone is usually left out of a game, or sitting alone because they are hurt. The life of Prince Siddhartha asks whether we will walk past.

## Notes
### Lessons that fit our age
We cannot copy his renunciation by leaving home. Children belong with their families. We can copy the direction of his heart:
- **Notice suffering.** Old age, sickness and sadness are not shameful. They are part of life. Do not mock a person who is ill or a grandparent who walks slowly.
- **Be kind while you still have enough.** Siddhartha did not wait until he was poor to care. Sharing a pencil or including someone in a game is a small form of the same movement.
- **Do not make fun of pain.** Laughing at a fall, a torn uniform or a classmate who learns slowly adds a second hurt.
- **Seek peace rather than only comfort.** The holy man he saw was peaceful without a palace. A quiet time of sitting still, or a choice not to join a cruel joke, is a beginning.
- **Tell the truth about what you saw.** He did not pretend the sick person was well. Honesty about a problem is the start of helping.

### Appreciation without pretending
You may be Sikh, Jain, Sanatan, Christian, Muslim or from another home. Appreciating Prince Siddhartha means you are glad this story exists and you will not mock Buddhists who honour him. Spiritual and moral growth can use a good example from another faith. You do not have to change your own worship to refuse cruelty.

### A reform we can join
The Buddha's later teaching reformed people's habits of hatred and carelessness. Even the childhood points that way. A class that stops name-calling has already implemented a piece of what his life asks.

## Key words
• compassion — caring about another person's suffering and wanting to help
• renunciation — giving up comforts in order to seek a higher good; not a step for children to take by leaving home

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A new learner sits alone because others say his speech is slow. What would a follower of Siddhartha's example do?

Working:
1. The prince was moved by suffering, not amused by it.
2. Invite the learner into the game or sit with him.
3. Tell an adult if the teasing continues. Do not copy it.

Answer: Include him, stop the teasing, and ask an adult for help if the unkindness goes on.

## Activity: A kindness watch
You will need: Exercise book
1. Discuss in groups what we learn from Prince Siddhartha. Write three lessons.
2. For one day, each learner notices one person who is left out, hurt or struggling with work.
3. Do one kind action: sit with them, explain the work, or tell a prefect or teacher if they are being bullied.
4. The next day, share what you did without naming anyone in a way that shames them.

## Practice
1. What do we learn from Prince Siddhartha about people who are sick or old?
2. Why should a Grade 4 learner not leave home to copy the prince?
3. Give one class rule that fits his example.

## Summary
• Prince Siddhartha teaches us to notice suffering and to be kind.
• Children stay at home; they copy his compassion, not his leaving the palace.
• Respecting his story is a way of growing morally.

### Answers to practice
1. We should not mock them. Their suffering deserves kindness.
2. Children are meant to stay in the care of their families. They practise kindness where they are.
3. Do not laugh at someone's pain, and include learners who are left out.

PAGE 8: Lesson 7: Sri Guru Ram Das Ji

LESSON 7: SRI GURU RAM DAS JI
=============================

## What you will learn
• Identify the contribution of Sri Guru Ram Das Ji.
• Explain how seva and humility were part of his life.

Curriculum outcomes: a) identify the contributions of Enlightened Beings for inspiration; b) implement teachings of Enlightened Beings for righteous living

## Introduction
The fourth Sikh Guru is remembered not for sitting above other people, but for serving them. Sri Guru Ram Das Ji shows that a leader can carry the heavy work and still be gentle.

## Notes
### From sevadar to Guru
Sri Guru Ram Das Ji is the fourth of the ten Sikh Gurus. Before he became Guru he was known as Bhai Jetha. He served in the langar and in the building work of the community. Sikh tradition remembers that he accepted humble tasks cheerfully, including carrying baskets of earth, when others wanted easier honour. Guru Amar Das Ji chose him as the next Guru because of that humility and love.

### Amritsar and the sarovar
He founded a settlement called Ramdaspur, later known as Amritsar. He began the sarovar, the holy pool, around which Sri Harmandir Sahib would rise. A pool that welcomes pilgrims is a reform of religious life: worship is not kept for a few important families. People come, bathe according to the custom, listen to kirtan and eat together.

### Words that are still sung
His hymns are part of Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji. Sikhs use his Lavan, the wedding hymn, in the Anand Karaj marriage ceremony. The hymn teaches a married couple to walk through life remembering God, not only pleasing themselves. Even learners who are years away from marriage can understand the idea: important promises should be made before God and kept with kindness.

### The contribution
His gift to the community was a place of worship and water, a tradition of seva, and scripture that is still recited. He did not teach people to boast. He taught them to work with their hands for others. That is why he is counted among the Enlightened Beings in this sub-strand.

## Key words
• Guru Ram Das Ji — the fourth Sikh Guru, founder of Ramdaspur (Amritsar)
• seva — selfless service
• langar — the free community kitchen in a gurdwara, where everyone sits as equals

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Which actions belong to Sri Guru Ram Das Ji: founding Ramdaspur and the sarovar, teaching the four restraints of Parshavnath, or appearing as a man-lion?

Working:
1. The man-lion is Narsimha Avtar.
2. The four restraints belong to Parshavnath.
3. Ramdaspur, the sarovar, seva and the Lavan belong to Guru Ram Das Ji.

Answer: Founding Ramdaspur and beginning the sarovar, together with seva and his hymns.

## Activity: Story of Guru Ram Das Ji
You will need: Audio or a reading chosen by the teacher
1. Listen to a short story of Sri Guru Ram Das Ji from a resource person, a parent or an audio device.
2. Write three contributions: humble seva, founding Ramdaspur and the sarovar, and hymns including the Lavan.
3. Match him on a chart with those contributions, and match the other Enlightened Beings with theirs so the names do not get mixed.
4. Discuss one line: how is seva still useful in a school?

## Practice
1. Which number Guru is Sri Guru Ram Das Ji?
2. What town did he found, and what is it called today?
3. What is seva, and how did he show it?

## Summary
• Sri Guru Ram Das Ji is the fourth Sikh Guru.
• He served humbly, founded Ramdaspur (Amritsar) and began the sarovar.
• His hymns, including the Lavan, are in Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji.

### Answers to practice
1. The fourth Sikh Guru.
2. He founded Ramdaspur, which became Amritsar.
3. Seva is selfless service. He served in the langar and did humble work such as carrying baskets of earth.

PAGE 9: Lesson 8: The Guru's teaching in modern life

LESSON 8: THE GURU'S TEACHING IN MODERN LIFE
============================================

## What you will learn
• Apply the teachings of Sri Guru Ram Das Ji at school and at home.
• Explain why his example still matters in a modern community.

Curriculum outcomes: b) implement teachings of Enlightened Beings for righteous living; c) appreciate the teachings of Enlightened Beings for spiritual and moral growth

## Introduction
Amritsar is far from your classroom, but a queue for food, a visitor who needs a seat, and a compound that needs cleaning are close. The key question asks how the teachings of Sri Guru Ram Das Ji fit modern society. They fit wherever people still need humility and service.

## Notes
### Seva has a modern shape
Guru Ram Das Ji did not ask for a comfortable job before he would help. Modern seva can look like these ordinary tasks:
- Wiping tables after a class meal without being pushed
- Carrying books for a learner who is on crutches
- Fetching water for visitors at a school function
- Joining a community clean-up instead of leaving the rubbish for someone poorer
- Letting an elder sit first, the way langar teaches people to sit as equals and to serve whoever comes

None of these needs a title. If you only help when a teacher is watching, the humility is still thin. The Guru served when the work was heavy and not glamorous.

### Equality
The sarovar and the langar were for all kinds of people. A modern school copies that reform when no learner is turned away from a game, a group or a shared meal because of tribe, faith, disability or the work their parents do. Mocking a classmate's lunch is the opposite of langar.

### Promises and pride
The Lavan teaches couples to remember God as they walk through life. For now, you can remember a smaller promise: if you say you will help, do it. Do not boast afterwards. Appreciation of the Guru grows when service stays quiet.

### All four beings in one week
Look back. Narsimha's story asks for faithful courage. Parshavnath asks for ahimsa. Prince Siddhartha asks you to notice suffering. Guru Ram Das Ji asks you to serve. A learner who practises even one of these each day is implementing the sub-strand, not only memorising names.

Write a short essay of one paragraph at home: which Enlightened Being you admire, what they contributed, and one action you will take. Read it to your family if they wish to hear it.

## Key words
• humility — not putting yourself above other people
• equality — treating people as having the same worth

## Worked examples

### Example 1
After a class party, plates are left on the floor. One learner says, 'That is the cleaner's work, not mine.' How does Guru Ram Das Ji's teaching answer?

Working:
1. He did humble work himself and did not wait for a lowly person to do it.
2. Helping to clear plates is seva.
3. The cleaner should still be treated kindly; the point is not to insult any worker, but not to refuse a fair share of the work.

Answer: Help clear the plates. Service is for everyone, and no worker should be despised.

## Activity: Short essay and a service task
You will need: Exercise book, A simple cleaning or helping task chosen by the teacher
1. Write a short essay: name one Enlightened Being, one contribution, and one way the teaching fits life now.
2. Read two essays aloud. Clap for effort, and correct any mix-up of names kindly.
3. Do one seva task together, such as sweeping the classroom or arranging chairs for a younger class. Include learners with special needs in roles they can do.
4. Finish by saying which teaching you appreciated most and why, without mocking the other faiths.

## Practice
1. Give two modern examples of seva a learner can do.
2. How does the idea of langar argue against mocking someone's food?
3. Why is Sri Guru Ram Das Ji still a useful example in modern society?

## Summary
• Guru Ram Das Ji's seva, humility and welcome still fit school life.
• Equality means nobody is shut out or mocked.
• Courage, ahimsa, compassion and service are the four teachings to practise.

### Answers to practice
1. Any two: cleaning the classroom, helping a classmate with special needs, serving visitors, or joining a clean-up.
2. Langar teaches that everyone sits as equals and is fed with respect, so shaming a person's food is against that teaching.
3. Communities still need humble leaders, places where all are welcome, and people who serve without pride.

REVISION QUIZ — 2.1 ENLIGHTENED BEINGS
========================================

Answer all the questions, then mark yourself on the Answers tab.

1. Which set names the four Enlightened Beings in this sub-strand?

pages.answers:
ANSWERS — 2.1 ENLIGHTENED BEINGS
========================================

1. A. Narsimha, Parshavnath, Prince Siddhartha, Guru Ram Das Ji
   The design names Narsimha Avtar, Parshavnath, Lord Buddha's childhood and Sri Guru Ram Das Ji.

2. B. Protect Prahlad from a cruel and proud king
   Vishnu came as the man-lion to protect the devotee Prahlad.

3. B. Stay truthful and faithful without becoming cruel
   The part to implement is faith and courage, not violence.

4. B. The twenty-third Jain Tirthankara
   Parshavnath is honoured in Jain tradition as the twenty-third Tirthankara.

5. A. Ahimsa, not harming living beings
   Ahimsa is the heart of his restraints, together with truth, not stealing and not being greedy.

6. B. Lumbini
   Buddhist tradition gives Lumbini as his birthplace. Bodh Gaya is where he later awakened.

7. We learn to notice suffering, to be kind, and not to mock people who are sick, old or sad.
   His sheltered childhood and the four sights turn him towards compassion.

8. A. Founding Ramdaspur, beginning the sarovar, and humble seva
   The fourth Guru served humbly and founded the settlement that became Amritsar.

9. By doing seva, such as cleaning or helping a classmate, without pride and without shutting anyone out.
   His humility, langar and welcome still apply wherever people live together.

10. B. Being glad of their teachings and growing in honesty, kindness and service
   Appreciation shows itself in respect and in moral growth.

studyPages.title: Overview
studyPages.body:
OVERVIEW
========

Enlightened Beings are holy teachers and divine forms whose lives guide people towards truth and goodness. In this sub-strand you will meet Narsimha Avtar, Parshavnath, the childhood of Lord Buddha, and Sri Guru Ram Das Ji. You will name what each one gave the world and practise those teachings in ordinary school life.

## Strand 2.0: Manifestations of Paramatma
Sub-strand 2.1: Enlightened Beings
Suggested lessons: 10

## Learning outcomes
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) identify the contributions of Enlightened Beings for inspiration
b) implement teachings of Enlightened Beings for righteous living
c) appreciate the teachings of Enlightened Beings for spiritual and moral growth

## What this sub-strand covers
• Narsimha Avtar
• Parshavnath
• Lord Buddha- His childhood
• Sri Guru Ram Das ji

## Key inquiry questions
1. Why are Enlightened Beings considered Divine?
2. What do we learn from the life of Prince Siddhartha?
3. How are the teachings of Sri Guru Ram Das Ji applicable in modern society?

## Core competencies
• Digital Literacy: Learner interacts with digital literacy when matching the Enlightened Beings with the reforms done by each (through dragging and dropping on digital device).
• Learning to learn: Learner learns independently when participating in short essay writing competition on Enlightened Beings.

## Values
• Respect: Learner enhances open-mindedness when performing skits based on the reforms done by Enlightened Beings.

## Pertinent and contemporary issues
• Citizenship: Learner is sensitised on human rights and responsibilities while matching the Enlightened Beings with the reforms done by each.

## Links to other learning areas
• Learner is able to link the skills of performing skits based on the reforms done by Enlightened Beings to the creative skills learnt in Creative Arts.

## Source
• KICD Grade 4 Hindu Religious Education Curriculum Design (Revised 2024) — Strand 2.0 Manifestations of Paramatma, Sub-strand 2.1 Enlightened Beings

studyPages.title: Lesson 1: Who Enlightened Beings are
studyPages.body:
LESSON 1: WHO ENLIGHTENED BEINGS ARE
====================================

## What you will learn
• Explain what is meant by an Enlightened Being in this sub-strand.
• Name the four Enlightened Beings to be studied.

Curriculum outcomes: a) identify the contributions of Enlightened Beings for inspiration; c) appreciate the teachings of Enlightened Beings for spiritual and moral growth

## Introduction
Stories of brave and holy lives are told at home, in the mandir, in the gurdwara and in the derasar. Hindu Religious Education calls some of these figures Enlightened Beings because their lives shine with truth and help other people live better.

## Notes
### A light for other people
To be enlightened means to see clearly what is true and what is right. An Enlightened Being may be a divine form of Paramatma, such as an avtar, or a human teacher who woke up to truth and then taught others. In both cases, people of faith look to that being for inspiration. Inspiration means a good example that makes you want to live bravely and kindly.

These beings are called divine by their communities because their lives are not ordinary stories of fame. They protect the weak, tell the truth, give up comfort for the sake of others, or build places where all people can worship together. Remembering them is a way of remembering God and goodness.

### The four you will study
This sub-strand names four:
- **Narsimha Avtar** — the man-lion form of Lord Vishnu in Sanatan tradition, remembered for protecting the child devotee Prahlad
- **Parshavnath** — the twenty-third Tirthankara of the Jains, a teacher of non-violence
- **Lord Buddha in his childhood** — Prince Siddhartha, before he became the Buddha
- **Sri Guru Ram Das Ji** — the fourth Guru of the Sikhs, remembered for humility and service

Each belongs to one of the four faiths you study. Learning one does not cancel the others. A respectful learner can admire Prahlad's courage and also admire Guru Ram Das Ji's service.

### How we will learn
You will hear short stories, match each being with a reform or a teaching, and try one teaching in class. A reform here means a change towards a fairer or holier way of living. Do not mix up their names. Narsimha is not a Sikh Guru, and Guru Ram Das Ji is not a Tirthankara.

## Key words
• enlightened — awake to truth; a guide whose life shows what is right
• avtar — a divine descent; a form in which God appears, in Sanatan teaching
• inspiration — a good example that encourages you to live better

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A learner says all four Enlightened Beings were Sikh Gurus. How should the list be corrected?

Working:
1. Only Sri Guru Ram Das Ji is a Sikh Guru, the fourth.
2. Narsimha Avtar belongs to Sanatan tradition.
3. Parshavnath is a Jain Tirthankara, and Prince Siddhartha is the future Buddha.

Answer: They come from four faiths: Sanatan, Jain, Buddhist and Sikh, one figure each.

## Activity: Match the Enlightened Being to the faith
You will need: Four name cards, Four faith cards
1. Spread out cards for Narsimha Avtar, Parshavnath, Prince Siddhartha and Sri Guru Ram Das Ji.
2. Match each name to Sanatan, Jain, Buddhist or Sikh.
3. With a partner, say one reason people of that faith honour the figure. If you are unsure, leave a question mark and listen to the coming lessons.
4. Help a classmate who needs the cards read aloud so that everyone can join the match.

## Practice
1. What does it mean to call someone an inspiration?
2. Name the four Enlightened Beings in this sub-strand.
3. Which of the four is a Jain Tirthankara?

## Summary
• Enlightened Beings guide people by their truth and goodness.
• This sub-strand studies Narsimha Avtar, Parshavnath, the childhood of the Buddha and Sri Guru Ram Das Ji.
• Each figure is kept with the correct faith.

### Answers to practice
1. Their example encourages other people to live in a better way.
2. Narsimha Avtar, Parshavnath, Lord Buddha as a child (Prince Siddhartha), and Sri Guru Ram Das Ji.
3. Parshavnath.

studyPages.title: Lesson 2: Narsimha Avtar and Prahlad
studyPages.body:
LESSON 2: NARSIMHA AVTAR AND PRAHLAD
====================================

## What you will learn
• Retell the story of Prahlad and Narsimha Avtar in the correct order.
• State what this avtar contributed for people of faith.

Curriculum outcomes: a) identify the contributions of Enlightened Beings for inspiration; c) appreciate the teachings of Enlightened Beings for spiritual and moral growth

## Introduction
Some children are pressed to do what they know is wrong. The Sanatan story of Prahlad tells of a boy who kept loving Lord Vishnu even when a powerful king tried to stop him. Vishnu came as Narsimha Avtar to protect him.

## Notes
### The king and the boy
Hiranyakashipu was a powerful king who wanted everyone to worship him. He had received a boon that made him feel safe from death: he was not to be killed by man or beast, not by day or by night, not indoors or outdoors, not on the earth or in the sky, and not by any weapon. His pride grew until he hated Lord Vishnu.

His own son, Prahlad, loved Vishnu. The boy chanted Vishnu's name at school and refused to say that the king was God. Hiranyakashipu tried again and again to turn him or to harm him. Prahlad stayed calm and faithful.

### The appearance of Narsimha
At last the king pointed to a pillar and mocked the idea that Vishnu could be in it. The pillar broke open. Narsimha appeared: a form that was neither a man nor a beast alone, but a man-lion. It was twilight, neither day nor night. Narsimha met the king on the threshold, which is neither fully inside nor fully outside, placed him on his lap, which is neither earth nor sky, and used claws rather than a weapon. The cruel king was destroyed. Prahlad was safe, and he asked mercy even for his father.

### The contribution
Narsimha Avtar is remembered as God's protection of a faithful child and as the defeat of pride and cruelty. The contribution is not a licence to be violent. It is a promise, in Sanatan teaching, that Paramatma stands with those who hold to truth, and that no boon can protect a person who harms the innocent.

Tell the story with respect. Do not act the killing in a frightening way in class. The part to copy is Prahlad's faith and his refusal to call a bully a god.

## Key words
• Narsimha — the man-lion avtar of Lord Vishnu
• Prahlad — the young devotee who stayed faithful to Vishnu
• boon — a special gift or promise, often from a deity after penance

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Why did Narsimha appear as a man-lion at twilight, on the threshold, using claws?

Working:
1. The king's boon blocked death by man or beast, by day or night, indoors or outdoors, on earth or in the sky, and by a weapon.
2. Each detail of the avtar meets the boon without breaking it.
3. The story teaches that pride cannot fence God out.

Answer: So that the proud king's boon could not stop the protection of Prahlad.

## Activity: Listen and retell the story of Narsimha
You will need: The story as told by a teacher, parent or audio recording
1. Listen to the story of Prahlad and Narsimha from your teacher, a parent or an audio device.
2. In groups, retell it in order: the proud king, the faithful boy, the pillar, the avtar, the safety of Prahlad.
3. Write one sentence on what this Enlightened Being contributes: protection of faith and the fall of cruelty.
4. Do not act violent blows. If you perform a sketch, end with Prahlad's prayer.

## Practice
1. Who was Prahlad, and whom did he worship?
2. What form did Lord Vishnu take to protect Prahlad?
3. What is the main contribution of this story for believers?

## Summary
• Prahlad stayed devoted to Vishnu when the king demanded worship for himself.
• Narsimha Avtar, the man-lion, protected Prahlad and ended the king's cruelty.
• The teaching is faith, courage and the defeat of pride.

### Answers to practice
1. He was the son of King Hiranyakashipu, and he worshipped Lord Vishnu.
2. Narsimha, the man-lion avtar.
3. It teaches that God protects a person who stays faithful, and that pride and cruelty do not last.

studyPages.title: Lesson 3: Living Prahlad's courage
studyPages.body:
LESSON 3: LIVING PRAHLAD'S COURAGE
==================================

## What you will learn
• Apply the teaching of Prahlad to situations at school.
• Choose truth and respect without insulting people who are powerful.

Curriculum outcomes: b) implement teachings of Enlightened Beings for righteous living; c) appreciate the teachings of Enlightened Beings for spiritual and moral growth

## Introduction
You may never face a king, but you may face a friend who says, 'Cheat with us, or we will leave you out.' Prahlad's story is told so that learners can answer that kind of pressure with a steady mind.

## Notes
### What to copy, and what not to copy
Prahlad did not gather a gang to fight his father. He told the truth, kept his prayer, and trusted Vishnu. Narsimha's appearance was God's act, not a plan for children to scratch or hit people. When we implement this teaching we practise faith, honesty and courage of speech. We do not practise cruelty.

### School situations
- Someone tells you to laugh at a classmate's faith or at the way they pray. You can refuse and change the subject.
- A group wants you to lie to the teacher about a broken window. You can tell the truth calmly.
- An older learner says you must give them your food. You can say no and walk to a teacher. Prahlad also spoke up; he did not pretend the king was right.
- You yourself have been proud and unkind. The story warns Hiranyakashipu's pride as much as it praises Prahlad. Apologise and start again.

### A calm voice
Courage can be quiet. A firm sentence is enough: 'I will not lie,' or 'I will not insult his prayer.' Shouting insults back is not devotion. Prahlad kept honouring Vishnu. He did not become a second bully.

### Appreciation
To appreciate this teaching is to be glad that faith can live inside a child, not only inside adults. Say thank you when you hear the story at home. If your family is not Sanatan, you can still respect the story and take the moral of honesty. Respect is part of spiritual growth.

## Key words
• implement — to put a teaching into practice
• devotion — steady love and loyalty towards God

## Worked examples

### Example 1
During group work, three learners copy answers and tell Asha to copy too, or they will say she is proud. What response fits Prahlad's example?

Working:
1. Copying and then lying is the wrong Prahlad refused, in a school form.
2. Asha can say no without insulting the group.
3. If they threaten her, she tells the teacher. She does not scratch or hit them.

Answer: She refuses to copy, speaks calmly, and reports the threat if it continues.

## Activity: A short skit on standing for the truth
You will need: Space to act, Three sentence cards
1. In small groups, choose one school pressure: cheating, mocking a faith, or taking someone's food.
2. Act a short skit in which one learner refuses calmly, as Prahlad refused the king's order.
3. End the skit with a helpful action, such as telling a teacher or apologising.
4. After each skit, the class names the teaching that was implemented.

## Practice
1. Name one way a learner can implement Prahlad's teaching at school.
2. Why should the class not copy the violent part of the Narsimha story?
3. What pride is warned against in the story of Hiranyakashipu?

## Summary
• Prahlad's example for school is truth, prayer and a calm refusal.
• Narsimha's act is God's, not a model for fighting.
• Appreciating the story means respecting devotion and rejecting pride.

### Answers to practice
1. Refuse to cheat or to mock someone's faith, and speak the truth calmly.
2. That moment belongs to the avtar's protection of Prahlad. Children are taught faith and courage, not cruelty.
3. The pride of demanding worship for yourself and harming a person who stays faithful to God.

studyPages.title: Lesson 4: Parshavnath, the twenty-third Tirthankara
studyPages.body:
LESSON 4: PARSHAVNATH, THE TWENTY-THIRD TIRTHANKARA
===================================================

## What you will learn
• Identify Parshavnath and his main teaching of non-violence.
• Give one way to practise that teaching.

Curriculum outcomes: a) identify the contributions of Enlightened Beings for inspiration; b) implement teachings of Enlightened Beings for righteous living

## Introduction
Long before modern wildlife clubs, Jain teachers were already saying that a small animal has a life you must not treat lightly. Parshavnath is honoured as the twenty-third Tirthankara, a guide who crossed beyond selfishness and showed others the way.

## Notes
### A Tirthankara
In Jain teaching, a Tirthankara is a person who has conquered anger, pride, greed and illusion and who builds a ford, a safe crossing, for others. Parshavnath is the twenty-third. Lord Mahavira, whom you meet when you study scriptures, is the twenty-fourth. Parshavnath is often shown with a canopy of snake hoods above him. The serpent is his emblem. It recalls a traditional account in which a serpent king sheltered him while he meditated, when he was attacked for his calm refusal to harm living beings.

### What he taught
Parshavnath taught householders and monks to restrain themselves. Four great restraints are remembered from his teaching:
- **Ahimsa** — do not injure living beings by thought, word or action
- **Satya** — speak the truth
- **Asteya** — do not steal or take what is not given
- **Aparigraha** — do not pile up more than you need

These are reforms of ordinary human habits. People often hurt others when they are angry, lie to escape trouble, take what they want, and cling to things. Parshavnath's contribution is a clear path of self-control.

### Implement ahimsa at Grade 4
You can practise without becoming a monk. Carry insects out of the classroom on a paper instead of crushing them when it is safe to do so. Do not throw stones at birds or dogs. Do not tear leaves off a living tree for fun. Speak in a way that does not wound a classmate. Ahimsa begins with the creatures and people you can reach today.

Appreciate this teaching by speaking of Parshavnath with his correct title, Tirthankara, and by not drawing his emblem as a joke.

## Key words
• Tirthankara — a Jain spiritual teacher who has crossed over and shows others the way
• Parshavnath — the twenty-third Jain Tirthankara, teacher of non-violence
• aparigraha — not holding on to more possessions than you need

## Worked examples

### Example 1
On the way home, learners hit a stray dog with sticks and laugh. Which restraint of Parshavnath does this break, and what should they do?

Working:
1. Harming an animal breaks ahimsa.
2. They should stop at once and leave the dog alone.
3. If the dog is hurt or dangerous, they tell an adult instead of attacking it.

Answer: It breaks ahimsa. They should stop, and tell an adult if the animal needs help.

## Activity: Match Parshavnath with his reforms
You will need: Cards for the four restraints, A picture of the snake emblem if one is available
1. Read a short account of Parshavnath told by your teacher or played on an audio device.
2. Match him with ahimsa, satya, asteya and aparigraha, and say each meaning in simple English.
3. Each learner chooses one restraint and writes one action they will do this week.
4. Assist a classmate who needs the words read aloud so they can make the same match.

## Practice
1. Who is Parshavnath?
2. What does ahimsa mean?
3. Name two restraints taught by Parshavnath besides ahimsa.

## Summary
• Parshavnath is the twenty-third Jain Tirthankara.
• He taught ahimsa, satya, asteya and aparigraha.
• Learners practise non-violence towards people, animals and plants.

### Answers to practice
1. The twenty-third Tirthankara in Jain tradition.
2. Non-violence: not harming living beings by thought, word or action.
3. Any two of satya (truth), asteya (not stealing) and aparigraha (not grabbing more than you need).

studyPages.title: Lesson 5: The childhood of Prince Siddhartha
studyPages.body:
LESSON 5: THE CHILDHOOD OF PRINCE SIDDHARTHA
============================================

## What you will learn
• Describe Prince Siddhartha's birth and sheltered childhood.
• Explain what his early life contributed to the story of the Buddha.

Curriculum outcomes: a) identify the contributions of Enlightened Beings for inspiration; c) appreciate the teachings of Enlightened Beings for spiritual and moral growth

## Introduction
Before he was called the Buddha, he was a prince in a palace. The key question of this sub-strand asks what we learn from the life of Prince Siddhartha. We begin with his childhood, not with later teachings he had not yet given.

## Notes
### Birth at Lumbini
Buddhist tradition says Prince Siddhartha Gautama was born at Lumbini. His father was King Suddhodana of the Shakya people, and his mother was Queen Maya. She died soon after his birth, and he was raised with love by Mahaprajapati Gautami, his mother's sister and the king's other queen. Wise visitors predicted that the child would become either a great ruler or a great sage.

### A palace without suffering in sight
The king wanted his son to choose the life of a ruler, so the boy was surrounded with comfort, beautiful gardens, fine clothes and pleasant company. He was trained in the skills of a prince. He was not cruel. Stories of his youth show a thoughtful boy who did not enjoy hurting living beings. He later married Yashodhara, and they had a son, Rahula. That family life still belongs to his early years, before he left the palace.

### What the comfort could not hide
As a young man he went out and saw four sights that his sheltered childhood had kept away: an old person, a sick person, a dead person, and a wandering holy man who looked peaceful. The first three showed him that comfort cannot cancel suffering. The fourth showed him a life given to seeking truth. He left the palace to understand suffering and the way beyond it. Years later, seated under the Boddhi tree, he awakened and was called the Buddha, the Awakened One.

### The contribution of the childhood story
The childhood itself is a gift to learners. It shows a child who had everything and still cared about pain that was not his own. People honour him as an Enlightened Being because that concern grew into a lifetime of teaching kindness, mindfulness and an end to cruelty. You do not need his palace in order to notice when someone in your class is left out or hurt.

## Key words
• Siddhartha — the prince who later became the Buddha
• Lumbini — the birthplace of Prince Siddhartha in Buddhist tradition
• Buddha — the Awakened One

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A learner says Prince Siddhartha was born poor and never lived in a palace. What does the childhood story actually say?

Working:
1. He was the son of King Suddhodana and Queen Maya.
2. He grew up with comfort in the palace and was protected from sights of suffering.
3. He left that comfort later, after seeing old age, sickness, death and a holy man.

Answer: He was a prince raised in comfort, and he left the palace when he saw suffering.

## Activity: Story of Prince Siddhartha's early life
You will need: A short reading or audio from the teacher
1. Listen to the childhood of Prince Siddhartha told by a resource person, a parent or an audio device.
2. Draw four small pictures: the birth and care by Mahaprajapati, life in the palace, the four sights, and a kind action of your own.
3. Under the drawing, write what we learn from his early life.
4. Watch only a film or video your teacher has chosen. Discuss one true fact from it, not a made-up scene.

## Practice
1. Where was Prince Siddhartha born, according to Buddhist tradition?
2. Who raised him after his mother, Queen Maya, died?
3. What four sights moved him to leave the palace?

## Summary
• Prince Siddhartha was born at Lumbini and raised in a palace after Queen Maya died.
• Comfort did not stop him from caring when he later saw suffering.
• His childhood leads towards his awakening as the Buddha.

### Answers to practice
1. At Lumbini.
2. Mahaprajapati Gautami.
3. An old person, a sick person, a dead person and a holy man.

studyPages.title: Lesson 6: What Prince Siddhartha teaches us now
studyPages.body:
LESSON 6: WHAT PRINCE SIDDHARTHA TEACHES US NOW
===============================================

## What you will learn
• List lessons from Prince Siddhartha's life for a Grade 4 learner.
• Show one of those lessons in a class activity.

Curriculum outcomes: b) implement teachings of Enlightened Beings for righteous living; c) appreciate the teachings of Enlightened Beings for spiritual and moral growth

## Introduction
A prince who notices suffering is a useful teacher for a school compound. Someone is usually left out of a game, or sitting alone because they are hurt. The life of Prince Siddhartha asks whether we will walk past.

## Notes
### Lessons that fit our age
We cannot copy his renunciation by leaving home. Children belong with their families. We can copy the direction of his heart:
- **Notice suffering.** Old age, sickness and sadness are not shameful. They are part of life. Do not mock a person who is ill or a grandparent who walks slowly.
- **Be kind while you still have enough.** Siddhartha did not wait until he was poor to care. Sharing a pencil or including someone in a game is a small form of the same movement.
- **Do not make fun of pain.** Laughing at a fall, a torn uniform or a classmate who learns slowly adds a second hurt.
- **Seek peace rather than only comfort.** The holy man he saw was peaceful without a palace. A quiet time of sitting still, or a choice not to join a cruel joke, is a beginning.
- **Tell the truth about what you saw.** He did not pretend the sick person was well. Honesty about a problem is the start of helping.

### Appreciation without pretending
You may be Sikh, Jain, Sanatan, Christian, Muslim or from another home. Appreciating Prince Siddhartha means you are glad this story exists and you will not mock Buddhists who honour him. Spiritual and moral growth can use a good example from another faith. You do not have to change your own worship to refuse cruelty.

### A reform we can join
The Buddha's later teaching reformed people's habits of hatred and carelessness. Even the childhood points that way. A class that stops name-calling has already implemented a piece of what his life asks.

## Key words
• compassion — caring about another person's suffering and wanting to help
• renunciation — giving up comforts in order to seek a higher good; not a step for children to take by leaving home

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A new learner sits alone because others say his speech is slow. What would a follower of Siddhartha's example do?

Working:
1. The prince was moved by suffering, not amused by it.
2. Invite the learner into the game or sit with him.
3. Tell an adult if the teasing continues. Do not copy it.

Answer: Include him, stop the teasing, and ask an adult for help if the unkindness goes on.

## Activity: A kindness watch
You will need: Exercise book
1. Discuss in groups what we learn from Prince Siddhartha. Write three lessons.
2. For one day, each learner notices one person who is left out, hurt or struggling with work.
3. Do one kind action: sit with them, explain the work, or tell a prefect or teacher if they are being bullied.
4. The next day, share what you did without naming anyone in a way that shames them.

## Practice
1. What do we learn from Prince Siddhartha about people who are sick or old?
2. Why should a Grade 4 learner not leave home to copy the prince?
3. Give one class rule that fits his example.

## Summary
• Prince Siddhartha teaches us to notice suffering and to be kind.
• Children stay at home; they copy his compassion, not his leaving the palace.
• Respecting his story is a way of growing morally.

### Answers to practice
1. We should not mock them. Their suffering deserves kindness.
2. Children are meant to stay in the care of their families. They practise kindness where they are.
3. Do not laugh at someone's pain, and include learners who are left out.

studyPages.title: Lesson 7: Sri Guru Ram Das Ji
studyPages.body:
LESSON 7: SRI GURU RAM DAS JI
=============================

## What you will learn
• Identify the contribution of Sri Guru Ram Das Ji.
• Explain how seva and humility were part of his life.

Curriculum outcomes: a) identify the contributions of Enlightened Beings for inspiration; b) implement teachings of Enlightened Beings for righteous living

## Introduction
The fourth Sikh Guru is remembered not for sitting above other people, but for serving them. Sri Guru Ram Das Ji shows that a leader can carry the heavy work and still be gentle.

## Notes
### From sevadar to Guru
Sri Guru Ram Das Ji is the fourth of the ten Sikh Gurus. Before he became Guru he was known as Bhai Jetha. He served in the langar and in the building work of the community. Sikh tradition remembers that he accepted humble tasks cheerfully, including carrying baskets of earth, when others wanted easier honour. Guru Amar Das Ji chose him as the next Guru because of that humility and love.

### Amritsar and the sarovar
He founded a settlement called Ramdaspur, later known as Amritsar. He began the sarovar, the holy pool, around which Sri Harmandir Sahib would rise. A pool that welcomes pilgrims is a reform of religious life: worship is not kept for a few important families. People come, bathe according to the custom, listen to kirtan and eat together.

### Words that are still sung
His hymns are part of Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji. Sikhs use his Lavan, the wedding hymn, in the Anand Karaj marriage ceremony. The hymn teaches a married couple to walk through life remembering God, not only pleasing themselves. Even learners who are years away from marriage can understand the idea: important promises should be made before God and kept with kindness.

### The contribution
His gift to the community was a place of worship and water, a tradition of seva, and scripture that is still recited. He did not teach people to boast. He taught them to work with their hands for others. That is why he is counted among the Enlightened Beings in this sub-strand.

## Key words
• Guru Ram Das Ji — the fourth Sikh Guru, founder of Ramdaspur (Amritsar)
• seva — selfless service
• langar — the free community kitchen in a gurdwara, where everyone sits as equals

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Which actions belong to Sri Guru Ram Das Ji: founding Ramdaspur and the sarovar, teaching the four restraints of Parshavnath, or appearing as a man-lion?

Working:
1. The man-lion is Narsimha Avtar.
2. The four restraints belong to Parshavnath.
3. Ramdaspur, the sarovar, seva and the Lavan belong to Guru Ram Das Ji.

Answer: Founding Ramdaspur and beginning the sarovar, together with seva and his hymns.

## Activity: Story of Guru Ram Das Ji
You will need: Audio or a reading chosen by the teacher
1. Listen to a short story of Sri Guru Ram Das Ji from a resource person, a parent or an audio device.
2. Write three contributions: humble seva, founding Ramdaspur and the sarovar, and hymns including the Lavan.
3. Match him on a chart with those contributions, and match the other Enlightened Beings with theirs so the names do not get mixed.
4. Discuss one line: how is seva still useful in a school?

## Practice
1. Which number Guru is Sri Guru Ram Das Ji?
2. What town did he found, and what is it called today?
3. What is seva, and how did he show it?

## Summary
• Sri Guru Ram Das Ji is the fourth Sikh Guru.
• He served humbly, founded Ramdaspur (Amritsar) and began the sarovar.
• His hymns, including the Lavan, are in Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji.

### Answers to practice
1. The fourth Sikh Guru.
2. He founded Ramdaspur, which became Amritsar.
3. Seva is selfless service. He served in the langar and did humble work such as carrying baskets of earth.

studyPages.title: Lesson 8: The Guru's teaching in modern life
studyPages.body:
LESSON 8: THE GURU'S TEACHING IN MODERN LIFE
============================================

## What you will learn
• Apply the teachings of Sri Guru Ram Das Ji at school and at home.
• Explain why his example still matters in a modern community.

Curriculum outcomes: b) implement teachings of Enlightened Beings for righteous living; c) appreciate the teachings of Enlightened Beings for spiritual and moral growth

## Introduction
Amritsar is far from your classroom, but a queue for food, a visitor who needs a seat, and a compound that needs cleaning are close. The key question asks how the teachings of Sri Guru Ram Das Ji fit modern society. They fit wherever people still need humility and service.

## Notes
### Seva has a modern shape
Guru Ram Das Ji did not ask for a comfortable job before he would help. Modern seva can look like these ordinary tasks:
- Wiping tables after a class meal without being pushed
- Carrying books for a learner who is on crutches
- Fetching water for visitors at a school function
- Joining a community clean-up instead of leaving the rubbish for someone poorer
- Letting an elder sit first, the way langar teaches people to sit as equals and to serve whoever comes

None of these needs a title. If you only help when a teacher is watching, the humility is still thin. The Guru served when the work was heavy and not glamorous.

### Equality
The sarovar and the langar were for all kinds of people. A modern school copies that reform when no learner is turned away from a game, a group or a shared meal because of tribe, faith, disability or the work their parents do. Mocking a classmate's lunch is the opposite of langar.

### Promises and pride
The Lavan teaches couples to remember God as they walk through life. For now, you can remember a smaller promise: if you say you will help, do it. Do not boast afterwards. Appreciation of the Guru grows when service stays quiet.

### All four beings in one week
Look back. Narsimha's story asks for faithful courage. Parshavnath asks for ahimsa. Prince Siddhartha asks you to notice suffering. Guru Ram Das Ji asks you to serve. A learner who practises even one of these each day is implementing the sub-strand, not only memorising names.

Write a short essay of one paragraph at home: which Enlightened Being you admire, what they contributed, and one action you will take. Read it to your family if they wish to hear it.

## Key words
• humility — not putting yourself above other people
• equality — treating people as having the same worth

## Worked examples

### Example 1
After a class party, plates are left on the floor. One learner says, 'That is the cleaner's work, not mine.' How does Guru Ram Das Ji's teaching answer?

Working:
1. He did humble work himself and did not wait for a lowly person to do it.
2. Helping to clear plates is seva.
3. The cleaner should still be treated kindly; the point is not to insult any worker, but not to refuse a fair share of the work.

Answer: Help clear the plates. Service is for everyone, and no worker should be despised.

## Activity: Short essay and a service task
You will need: Exercise book, A simple cleaning or helping task chosen by the teacher
1. Write a short essay: name one Enlightened Being, one contribution, and one way the teaching fits life now.
2. Read two essays aloud. Clap for effort, and correct any mix-up of names kindly.
3. Do one seva task together, such as sweeping the classroom or arranging chairs for a younger class. Include learners with special needs in roles they can do.
4. Finish by saying which teaching you appreciated most and why, without mocking the other faiths.

## Practice
1. Give two modern examples of seva a learner can do.
2. How does the idea of langar argue against mocking someone's food?
3. Why is Sri Guru Ram Das Ji still a useful example in modern society?

## Summary
• Guru Ram Das Ji's seva, humility and welcome still fit school life.
• Equality means nobody is shut out or mocked.
• Courage, ahimsa, compassion and service are the four teachings to practise.

### Answers to practice
1. Any two: cleaning the classroom, helping a classmate with special needs, serving visitors, or joining a clean-up.
2. Langar teaches that everyone sits as equals and is fed with respect, so shaming a person's food is against that teaching.
3. Communities still need humble leaders, places where all are welcome, and people who serve without pride.

questions.question: Which set names the four Enlightened Beings in this sub-strand?
options: Narsimha, Parshavnath, Prince Siddhartha, Guru Ram Das Ji
Mahavira, Guru Nanak, Rama, Krishna only
questions.explanation: The design names Narsimha Avtar, Parshavnath, Lord Buddha's childhood and Sri Guru Ram Das Ji.

questions.question: Narsimha Avtar appeared in order to
options: Protect Prahlad from a cruel and proud king
questions.explanation: Vishnu came as the man-lion to protect the devotee Prahlad.

questions.question: Prahlad's example teaches a learner to
options: Worship a bully if the bully is strong
Stay truthful and faithful without becoming cruel
Hide every mistake with a lie
questions.explanation: The part to implement is faith and courage, not violence.

questions.question: Parshavnath is
questions.explanation: Parshavnath is honoured in Jain tradition as the twenty-third Tirthankara.

questions.question: Which teaching belongs to Parshavnath?
options: Breaking a pillar as a man-lion
Demanding that everyone worship a king
questions.explanation: Ahimsa is the heart of his restraints, together with truth, not stealing and not being greedy.

questions.question: Prince Siddhartha was born at
options: Bodh Gaya, as a baby in the story's first scene
questions.explanation: Buddhist tradition gives Lumbini as his birthplace. Bodh Gaya is where he later awakened.

questions.question: What do we learn from the life of Prince Siddhartha?
questions.answer: We learn to notice suffering, to be kind, and not to mock people who are sick, old or sad.
questions.explanation: His sheltered childhood and the four sights turn him towards compassion.

questions.question: Sri Guru Ram Das Ji is remembered for
options: Founding Ramdaspur, beginning the sarovar, and humble seva
questions.explanation: The fourth Guru served humbly and founded the settlement that became Amritsar.

questions.question: How can Guru Ram Das Ji's teaching be used in a school today?
questions.answer: By doing seva, such as cleaning or helping a classmate, without pride and without shutting anyone out.
questions.explanation: His humility, langar and welcome still apply wherever people live together.

questions.question: Appreciating Enlightened Beings means
options: Mocking the faith you do not follow
Being glad of their teachings and growing in honesty, kindness and service
Mixing up their stories on purpose
Copying only the violent parts of a story
questions.explanation: Appreciation shows itself in respect and in moral growth.
